approved: Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Television and Radio Licence Fees) Bill 2016

The majority voted to agree with the bill's main idea, which means the Senate can now discuss the bill in more detail. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### Bill's main idea The [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5721) was introduced to reduce licence fees that commercial television broadcasting licensees and commercial radio broadcasting licensees have to pay by 25 per cent. According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd015): > *The free-to-air broadcasters would like to see licence fees abolished altogether. They argue this would better enable them to fulfil their local content obligations and assist them to remain financially viable in a new media environment where subscription and online media operators do not pay licence fees.* > *Subscription broadcasters argue that reducing licensing fees for free-to-air commercial broadcasters amounts to preferential treatment as the free-to-air operators are being given discounts to use the public resource of spectrum, while also enjoying market protection as the result of other government regulation.* > *Some stakeholders argue that licence fee reductions should be accompanied by reciprocal requirements to increase local content production, but this is not a feature of this Bill.*

The bill proposes a permanent 25 per cent reduction in licence fees for commercial television and radio broadcasters, amending the Television Licence Fees Act 1964 and Radio Licence Fees Act 1964 to set fees at 75 per cent of the amount otherwise due, effective from the 2015–16 financial year. The argument is that this will help broadcasters compete with online operators like Netflix and Apple, which pay no licence fees, and continue investing in Australian content and local jobs.

The bill reduces commercial television and radio licence fees by 25 per cent, from 4.5 per cent to 3.375 per cent of gross revenue, providing an estimated $163 million in relief. The speaker argued this is necessary due to competition from unregulated online platforms like Netflix, Google, and Facebook, and noted that Australian licence fees are higher than in comparable countries.

The bill reduces commercial television and radio licence fees by 25 per cent, part of a broader package to help traditional media compete with internet-based rivals, with the measure costing $163 million over the forward estimates. The reduction is from a maximum rate of 4.5 per cent for television and 3.25 per cent for radio, compared with under 0.2 per cent in Britain.

Labor supported the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Television and Radio Licence Fees) Bill 2016, which reduces annual licence fees for commercial free-to-air broadcasters from 4.5% to 3.375% of gross revenue. The speech cited a 15% decline in free-to-air TV viewership since 2008 and the rise of streaming services like Netflix, and called for investigation into tax avoidance by companies such as Google.

The speaker argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Television and Radio Licence Fees) Bill 2016 should permanently reduce commercial television and radio licence fees by 25% from the 2015‑16 financial year, to help broadcasters compete with online services like Netflix and Facebook that pay no licence fees, and to support local news, content and jobs in regional Australia.

The member for Shortland argued that many constituents in her electorate suffer from poor digital television reception, including regular cut-outs and channel failures, which worsened after the digital switchover. She criticised the Prime Minister for providing $800,000 to address similar issues in the Liberal-held seat of Paterson while ignoring Shortland, and called on broadcasters to invest licence fee savings into infrastructure.

The speech supported the bill to reduce television and radio licence fees, noting that $163 million in revenue would be lost over four years while multinational competitors like Netflix and Apple pay no fees. The speaker called for $2.2 million per year in government support for community broadcasters such as Adelaide’s Channel 44 and stations in the Mayo electorate.

The bill reduces commercial television and radio licence fees by 25% as included in the 2016-17 budget, to help broadcasters compete with online media that pay no fees. The speaker urged passage by 31 December to ease financial burdens on traditional and regional broadcasters.
